questions.q: What is the basic experimental setup in weak-to-strong generalization research?
options: Training two identical models on the exact same ground-truth labels
Fine-tuning a weak model on a task, then using its (sometimes mistaken) labels to train a much stronger pretrained model on that same task, instead of ground-truth labels
Having a strong model grade its own outputs with no supervision at all
Deleting all weak models from the study before training begins
questions.explain: This setup simulates the weak-supervising-strong problem using models available today, with the weak model's labels standing in for imperfect human supervision.

questions.q: What role does ground truth play in this research, given that it isn't used to train the strong model?
options: It plays no role at all in the study
It's available to researchers for grading purposes afterward, letting them measure how well the strong model generalized beyond the weak supervisor's mistakes
It is used to train the weak model exclusively, never for evaluation
It replaces the weak model's labels entirely during training
questions.explain: Ground truth is withheld from the training signal but used afterward to measure the real performance gap and how much of it the strong model recovered.

questions.q: What would naive fine-tuning on a weak supervisor's labels be expected to do to a strong model's performance, absent any special generalization?
options: Push the strong model's performance far above the weak supervisor's performance automatically
Cap the strong model's performance at roughly the weak supervisor's own performance, since that is what it is being trained to imitate
Have no measurable effect on the strong model's performance whatsoever
Always cause the strong model to fail completely on the task
questions.explain: Naively, a student trained to match a teacher's labels would be expected to match the teacher's performance level, not exceed it, absent extra generalization.

questions.q: What was the main empirical finding of OpenAI's weak-to-strong generalization work?
options: Strong models trained on weak labels often perform better than the weak supervisor, recovering a meaningful but partial fraction of the gap to the strong model's true ceiling
Strong models always perform identically to the weak supervisor with no improvement
Strong models trained on weak labels always perform worse than random guessing
The gap between weak and strong model performance was fully and completely closed in every task tested
questions.explain: The recovery is real and encouraging but explicitly partial, varying across tasks and model pairs rather than being a complete, uniform solution.

questions.q: How does this lesson characterize the open questions around weak-to-strong generalization?
options: There are no open questions; the result is considered a fully solved and complete answer to scalable oversight
Whether the partial recovery seen today will hold as the capability gap between supervisor and system grows and tasks get harder is explicitly flagged as unresolved by the researchers themselves
The only open question is which programming language was used to run the experiments
The result has been proven false and fully retracted by the original researchers
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this is framed as an early, imperfect analogy, with real open questions about how the finding generalizes to the actual future problem it approximates.
